front: Name the main funding sources for a government budget deficit.
back: Taxes, borrowing (bond issuance) and monetary financing (central bank money creation). Most deficits are financed by borrowing; heavy monetary financing risks inflation.
Total government debt ÷ nominal GDP. It rises when deficits are financed by borrowing faster than nominal GDP grows.
P = F × (1 − d × t/360), where d is the discount rate. Money market yield = (F − P)/P × 360/t, which is higher than the discount rate.

front: Compare bills, notes/bonds, FRNs and inflation-linked bonds.
back: Bills: one year or less, discount, no coupon. Notes/bonds: fixed coupons. FRNs: reference rate + spread. Inflation-linked: principal indexed to inflation, pays a real yield.
Adjusted principal = par × index ratio; coupon = adjusted principal × real coupon rate ÷ periods per year.
Single-price (Dutch): all winners pay the stop-out price/yield. Multiple-price: each winner pays their own bid.
A bank or securities firm obliged to bid at government auctions and make secondary markets, in exchange for privileged access to the issuer.
On-the-run: the most recently auctioned issue of a maturity; most liquid. Off-the-run: older issues; less liquid. On-the-run yields form the benchmark curve.

front: How is a non-sovereign bond yield built from the benchmark?
back: Yield = benchmark government yield of the same maturity + spread (credit, liquidity and other risk premium).
Paid-in and callable capital from member countries, plus preferred creditor status. Usually AAA-rated.

front: General obligation versus revenue municipal bonds
back: GO: repaid from general taxing power. Revenue: repaid from a specific project's cash flows.
Tax-exempt yield ÷ (1 − marginal tax rate). Example: 3.60% ÷ 0.68 = 5.29% at a 32% tax rate.
